references.text: Malachi asks why the people call God "Lord" yet do not honor him with their actions—the same tension between confession and obedience that Jesus points to.

Jesus' parallel statement in Matthew: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the one who does the will of my Father in heaven." This is the closest parallel to Luke 6:46.
The foolish bridesmaids cry out, "Lord, Lord, open up for us!" but are rejected—illustrating that confession without preparation and obedience is not enough.
Paul emphasizes that it is not those who hear the law who are righteous before God, but those who do what the law says—the same principle that action must follow confession.
James urges believers to be doers of the word, not merely hearers—this reflects Jesus' point that it profits nothing to call him Lord without doing what he says.
James teaches that faith without works is dead—a confession without action has no value, which directly corresponds with Jesus' rebuke.
John writes that whoever says "I know him" but does not keep his commandments is a liar—this expands on the tension between verbal confession and actual obedience.
The immediately following passage in Luke where Jesus illustrates this point with the parable of the two builders—the one who hears and acts versus the one who hears but does not act.

Jesus warns that some will say, "We ate and drank with you," but he will reply, "I do not know where you are from"—again highlighting the distinction between outward association and genuine obedience.
